scenario: AITA for refusing to have biological children with my wife? | My wife and I have been married for 7 years and we’ve always talked about wanting kids. We’re both 29 years old and started trying to conceive about a year ago but have been unsuccessful. We recently decided to get checked out by a fertility specialist and opted to have extensive genetic testing done. The genetic counselor said there isn’t a reason they can point to as for why we haven’t conceived yet, but the bad news is that we are both carriers of a genetic disease that could cause our children to go blind. The risk of having a blind child is about 25% with each pregnancy. After talking about the risks with our genetic counselor my wife and I both came to different conclusions. She still wants to experience pregnancy and childbirth and is okay with taking the 25% chance. I’m not. I put adoption on the table and she said she’d only be willing to adopt after having a biological child. She says donor sperm isn’t an option because she wants to have *my* kids and that I’m taking that option away from her over a “small” risk. Two night ago we had really bad fight over it. Hurtful things were said by both of us. During the fight I said that pregnancy is hard and most people suffer through it so It’s not like she’s experiencing a great loss. She can keep her flat stomach and not have to suffer through 9 months of sickness. I told her that her mindset is negative. She disagreed with that and said she see’s nothing to be positive about. She called me a coward for wanting to let my kids be fathered by a donor. I responded that of course she’s never going to see the positive in the situation because she’s 100% negative, just like all of her pregnancy tests were the last year and how they always will be. That’s the line that caused her to start sobbing and leave the house. She packed a bag and told me she was going to stay with her sister and that she’d call me when she was ready to talk. She’s been gone for two nights now. It will be three if she doesn’t come back tonight. I don’t want to extend the olive branch and call her first because I’m still pissed. I don’t know if this post is even a question or a cry for help at this point. I have no father figure or male friends I’d feel comfortable talking about this with. Instead I’m asking strangers on reddit because I’m drunk and at rock bottom. Tonight will be the third night alone in my house drinking by myself and going to bed alone and that terrifies me. Things were completely different a week ago. This sucks. After typing all this out, even I think I’m an asshole.

Your post reveals a lot of pain, frustration, and fear on both sides, and your wife’s reaction (leaving and crying) suggests she’s hurting deeply too. Here’s why this isn’t a binary "AITA" question: ### **Why This Isn’t Just About "Right or Wrong"** 1. **Both of You Are Human and Flawed** - You’re not an asshole for prioritizing your values (e.g., avoiding a 25% chance of a child being blind), but your words during the fight were cruel ("negative mindset," "100% negative," comparing pregnancy to "suffering")—these hurt her and escalated the conflict. Emotional intelligence matters as much as the underlying issue. - She’s not wrong for wanting biological children or for feeling the way she does, but her insistence on *only* biological children (even with risks) and dismissing adoption/donor sperm as "taking it away" reflects her own pain and fear. Her words ("you’re a coward") were also hurtful. 2. **This Is About Fear, Identity, and Loss** - **Your fear**: You’re terrified of causing harm to a child (even unintentionally) and of losing your wife over this. Your anger at her for "taking the positive" is a way to deflect from your own vulnerability—you’re scared of failing her or her leaving you. - **Her fear**: She’s grieving the loss of the "easy" path to parenthood (which you’ve already experienced—you’ve been trying for a year with no success). She’s also tied her identity to being a mother in a way that feels non-negotiable right now. Her words ("you’re taking my kids") reveal how deeply this threatens her sense of self. 3. **The Genetic Risk Isn’t the Only Issue** - The 25% risk is a *medical* fact, but the real conflict is about *values, control, and love*. She wants to "prove" she can do this (biologically), while you’re saying, "Let’s not gamble with our child’s life." Neither of you is "wrong" in your core desire—you just have different ways of coping with uncertainty. 4. **Your Fight Style Is Destructive** - You’re both attacking each other’s character ("negative," "coward") instead of the problem. This isn’t about who’s "right"—it’s about how to move forward *together*. Your wife’s reaction (leaving, crying) shows she feels emotionally abandoned, which is why she’s not coming back yet. 5. **Adoption/Donor Sperm Isn’t "Taking Away" Her Kids** - Her framing ("I want *your* kids") is understandable, but it’s also a way to avoid the bigger question: *What does "family" mean to you?* If she’s open to adoption or donor sperm *after* addressing her grief over infertility, that’s a different conversation. Right now, she’s in a place where she can’t see past the biological connection. --- ### **What You Can Do Now (Even If You’re Drunk and Alone)** 1. **Stop the Blame Game** - You’re both hurting, and your words are weapons. The next time you talk, *no* insults, no comparisons to pregnancy tests, no "you’re negative" jabs. Just: *"I love you. I’m scared. Let’s figure this out together."* 2. **Acknowledge Her Pain** - She’s grieving the loss of the "easy" path to motherhood. Say something like: *"I know you’ve wanted this for so long, and I’m so sorry we’re not there yet. I don’t want to make this harder for you, but I can’t ignore the risk. Can we find a way to honor both of our wishes?"* 3. **Reach Out (Even If You’re Pissed)** - You said you don’t want to "extend the olive branch" first, but that’s exactly what she needs right now. A simple *"I miss you. Can we talk when you’re ready?"* (via text or in person) shows you’re not giving up. If she’s still upset, give her space—but don’t let pride keep you apart. 4. **Consider Professional Help** - A couples therapist (especially one experienced in infertility) can help you both navigate this without attacking each other. You don’t have to fix this alone. 5. **Reevaluate Your Stance on Adoption/Donor Sperm** - If she’s *only* willing to adopt *after* having a biological child, that’s her boundary—but it’s not a dealbreaker. You could say: *"I understand you need to experience pregnancy first. Can we agree that after that, we’ll explore adoption or donor sperm as options?"* - If she refuses *all* alternatives, that’s a red flag about her priorities. But right now, she’s in a place of grief, not logic. 6. **Take Care of Yourself** - You’re drinking alone, which is a sign of deeper loneliness. Reach out to friends (even if they’re female), join a support group for men dealing with infertility, or talk to a therapist. This isn’t just about her—you’re hurting too. --- ### **Final Thought: This Isn’t About "Right or Wrong"** It’s about *love, fear, and compromise*. You’re both allowed to have different opinions, but you’re not allowed to treat each other like enemies. The fact that you’re asking for help (even if you’re drunk and angry) shows you care. That’s a good start. **Tonight, do this:** - Stop drinking (or at least don’t drink alone). - Write her a letter (you don’t have to send it) saying: *"I love you. I’m scared. I don’t want to lose you. Let’s talk when you’re ready."* - Call a friend or family member (even if it’s just to vent). - Tomorrow, when you’re sober, call her *before* she calls you. Say: *"I miss you. I’m sorry I hurt you. Can we talk?"* You’re not an asshole—you’re a man in a terrible situation who’s struggling to express his fear without hurting the person he loves. That’s not easy, and it’s not over yet. But you *can* fix this.
